title: The County Prosecutors Who Became ICE Informants
gist: An Injustice Watch/WIRED investigation of over 5,000 pages of FOIA'd emails finds that state's attorneys' offices in roughly 1 in 6 Illinois counties voluntarily fed federal immigration agents defendants' personal data, court dates, and release times despite Illinois's 2017 TRUST Act 'sanctuary' law, exposing a legal loophole (prosecutors are arguably not bound by a law written for police) that other sanctuary states likely share.

insights.claim: Illinois's 2017 TRUST Act bars police and sheriffs from helping federal agents with deportation absent a criminal warrant, but the law does not clearly specify whether county prosecutors and their staff are bound by the same restriction, creating a legal gray zone prosecutors exploited.
insights.speaker: Aura Bogado
insights.so_what: This is a generalizable structural gap: any 'sanctuary' statute modeled on limiting police/sheriff cooperation (as most are) may leave prosecutorial offices — which control case files, court dates, and release schedules — entirely uncovered, meaning similar workarounds likely exist in other sanctuary states and cities.
insights.quote: The TRUST Act bars police and other agencies from helping federal agents deport people absent a federal criminal warrant. But the law doesn't squarely answer whether prosecutors and their staff are bound by those same restrictions.
insights.locator: The TRUST Act bars police and other agencies

insights.claim: State's attorneys' offices in 1 out of every 6 Illinois counties acted as assets to federal immigration enforcement, sharing sensitive personal data on people they were prosecuting without warrants, public disclosure, or legislative oversight, and with no tracking of how often it happened.
insights.speaker: Aura Bogado
insights.so_what: A roughly 17% institutional-participation rate, entirely undisclosed and untracked, is the kind of hidden base rate an investor/policy analyst modeling 'sanctuary state' protections should treat as a material discount to headline legal protections in any jurisdiction with similar gaps.
insights.locator: State's attorneys offices in 1 out of every 6 Illinois counties

insights.claim: Neither DuPage County (which cooperated most) nor Lake County (which refused entirely) tracks its contacts with ICE, and state's attorneys are not required to file the annual TRUST Act compliance reports that police departments and sheriffs must file.
insights.speaker: Aura Bogado
insights.so_what: The absence of a reporting requirement specifically for prosecutors (unlike police) is the structural root cause enabling undetected cooperation — a clean legislative fix (extend reporting mandates to prosecutors) that advocacy groups will likely push for next.
insights.locator: Neither office tracks its contact with ICE

insights.claim: The two Illinois offices with the clearest public positions landed on opposite legal theories: DuPage's Bob Berlin said his office is bound by the TRUST Act yet cooperated with ICE more than any other county; Lake County's Eric Rinehart said his office is not bound by the Act (since it doesn't arrest or detain people) yet voluntarily refused all cooperation anyway.
insights.speaker: Aura Bogado
insights.so_what: Legal coverage and actual behavior are inverted between these two offices, showing that individual prosecutorial discretion — not statutory text — is the operative variable; this undercuts confidence that passing a stronger law alone would change outcomes without also constraining discretion.
insights.locator: These two offices staked out the clearest positions

insights.claim: DuPage County — where 1 in 5 residents were born abroad — had the highest volume of prosecutor-ICE contact in the state, with staff both answering federal information requests and proactively offering specific cases for agents to pursue.
insights.speaker: Aura Bogado
insights.so_what: High-immigrant-population counties being simultaneously the highest-cooperation counties is a counter-intuitive finding — worth watching if it reflects higher case volume generally or an active enforcement targeting pattern.
insights.locator: According to documents reviewed by Injustice Watch, contact happened more often in DuPage County

insights.claim: In one case, a CBP officer's administrative subpoena (issued by DHS, not a judge, and carrying no independent legal force unless a federal court enforced it) for voter-fraud-related records was fulfilled by a DuPage prosecutor within 90 minutes, without pushing back or requiring judicial backing.
insights.speaker: Aura Bogado
insights.so_what: Administrative subpoenas function as de facto compulsory process because local officials comply voluntarily rather than testing their legal weight — a mechanism worth flagging in any analysis of how federal agencies expand practical authority without new legislation or court orders.

insights.claim: Kane County prosecutors asked Customs and Border Protection to identify three people using facial recognition technology, which the state's attorney characterized as 'a standard investigatory technique used throughout all of law enforcement.'
insights.speaker: Aura Bogado
insights.so_what: Local prosecutors routing facial-recognition requests through federal immigration agents (rather than an in-state law-enforcement database) is a specific surveillance-technology usage pattern relevant to debates on facial-recognition governance and interagency data-sharing controls.
insights.quote: a standard investigatory technique used throughout all of law enforcement.
insights.locator: In Kane County, where staffers asked Customs and Border Protection

insights.claim: Because civil deportation proceedings require only 'clear and convincing evidence' versus the 'beyond a reasonable doubt' standard in criminal cases and offer no guaranteed appointed counsel, some local officials may be incentivized to route defendants to ICE to 'clear their docket' rather than prosecute, per a former DHS lawyer.
insights.speaker: Aura Bogado
insights.so_what: This is the core incentive-structure insight: handing a defendant to ICE is procedurally easier than winning a criminal conviction, so cost/efficiency pressure on local prosecutors' offices can systematically funnel people into the weaker-rights civil track — a mechanism that generalizes beyond Illinois wherever criminal and immigration systems intersect.
insights.locator: Spencer Reynolds, an attorney with the NAACP Legal Defense Fund

insights.claim: Marion County prosecutor John Christeson emailed a Homeland Security Investigations agent details on defendant Rolando Perez Samayoa (date of birth, court date, home address); three weeks later federal agents arrested Samayoa at his home and detained his 17-year-old son as well.
insights.speaker: Aura Bogado
insights.so_what: This is the investigation's clearest documented causal chain from a prosecutor's email to a specific family's detention and removal — the kind of concrete case record that typically drives subsequent litigation, legislative amendment, or disciplinary action.
insights.quote: Ok, we'll take care of it, thank you

insights.claim: Neither defendants nor their defense attorneys were aware, in nearly all documented cases, that prosecutors were sharing case information with federal immigration agents — meaning the practice operated entirely outside adversarial visibility.
insights.speaker: Aura Bogado
insights.so_what: A total information asymmetry (defense counsel unaware of a channel actively being used against their client) undermines the basic adversarial-process assumption the criminal justice system depends on — a structural due-process concern beyond the immigration-policy question itself.
insights.locator: Nearly all the defense attorneys whose clients appear in the records

insights.claim: A University of Kentucky law professor said he could not recall a single instance in his past practice of a state's attorney's office sharing information with ICE, calling the scale of Illinois prosecutor collaboration found in this investigation unprecedented.
insights.speaker: Aura Bogado
insights.so_what: An outside legal expert's framing of the pattern as historically unprecedented supports treating this as a genuine new phenomenon in the second Trump term's immigration enforcement — not a longstanding practice merely newly documented — with implications for how the administration is operationalizing enforcement through under-scrutinized channels.
insights.quote: I cannot recall a single instance in my past practice where an individual within the state's attorney's office shared information with ICE.
